subject: biology
title: Ecology Adventure 3: Climate change and conservation
welcome_lead: Today you'll tackle climate change and the biodiversity crisis.
meta_desc: Biology — greenhouse effect, climate change evidence, ocean acidification, conservation.
final_note: You learned CO₂ and CH₄ trap IR radiation, raising global temperatures, acidifying oceans and shifting ecosystems — biodiversity loss is the 6th mass extinction.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Sun emits short-wave UV/visible — reaches Earth's surface.

Earth re-emits long-wave infrared. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb IR and re-emit in all directions — warming the lower atmosphere.

Without it, Earth's average T ≈ -18°C. With it, +15°C. Enhanced effect from fossil fuels → ~1.1°C warming since 1900 (IPCC AR6).

About 30% of emitted CO₂ dissolves in oceans:

CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.

Ocean pH has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1 since 1750 (≈30% more H⁺). This dissolves CaCO₃ shells, threatening coral reefs (e.g. Great Barrier Reef bleaching events 2016, 2017, 2020).

Species are vanishing at 100-1000× background rate — the 6th mass extinction.

Conservation:
- In-situ — national parks (Yellowstone 1872, Serengeti).
- Ex-situ — zoos, seed banks (Svalbard Global Seed Vault).

nature of science: science informs policy, but value judgements (intrinsic value of species, equity between nations) belong to society.

Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
options: X-linked recessive conditions affect more males because the Y chromosome makes the disease worse.
X-linked conditions affect only males because females cannot inherit X-linked alleles.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
X-linked conditions affect only males because females cannot inherit X-linked alleles.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.
